Committee Members O’Connell, Parr, Smith,   Aldermanic Chambers  
Superintendent (or designee) and Rep. Suzanne Chretien City Hall, 3 rd Floor 
 
 
1. Chair O’Connell calls the meeting to order.  
 
2. The Clerk calls the roll.  
 
3. Public Forum 
 
4. Chair O’Connell advises that the purpose of the public forum is to give the residents of 
Manchester the opportunity to address the board on items of concerns affecting the community; 
each person will be given only one opportunity to speak; comments shall be limited to three 
minutes to allow all participants the opportunity to speak and any comments must be directed 
to the Chair. Speakers may offer comments on school operations and programs that concern 
them.  
 
5. Chair O’Connell advises that if there was no one else present wishing to speak, a motion would

Manchester Board of School Committee 
Manchester School District ~ SAU 37 
20 Hecker Street, Manchester, NH 03102    
 
 
 
October 14, 2026           
 
Re: HB1300  
 
Dear Secretary Scanlan, Attorney General Formella, and Commissioner Stepp, 
       
We, the Manchester Board of School Committee, are writing about the implementation of HB 1300, now 
RSA 32:5-i. On November 3, voters in every New Hampshire community will answer the school tax cap 
question it requires. We are not writing about how anyone should vote. We are writing because the 
statute leaves basic questions unanswered, and the school boards that will have to carry out the result 
cannot yet answer them. 
 
The New Hampshire School Boards Association has advised its members that, as of October 1, neither 
the Secretary of State's Office nor the Attorney General's Office had issued guidance on several of these 
questions, some of which bear on our district: 
 
 Who certifies the result? RSA 32:5-i directs ward moderators to report results to the "secretary 
of the school administrative unit board," who certifies them to DRA and schedules any recount. 
Manchester is a single-district SAU. Under RSA 194-C:3 it is not required to have that officer, and 
the statute does not say who acts in its place. Many other single-district SAUs are in the same 
position. 
 
 How is a cap overridden in a city district? The statute's override provisions are written around 
districts with an annual meeting. City districts without one, including Manchester, cannot tell from 
the text how an adopted cap would be overridden, or how it would interact with an existing charter 
cap, since the statute requires that every applicable limitation be satisfied. 
 
 What counts as the "central office administrative budget"?  The 6% SAU cap uses a 
definition that does not match the services SAUs must already provide under RSA 194-C:4 and 
194-C:9. SAUs cannot build a compliant budget for FY 2028 without knowing what the cap 
measures. 
 
We respectfully ask for three things: 
 
1. From the Secretary of State and the Attorney General:  written guidance, before results must 
be certified, on who performs the SAU secretary's duties in single-district SAUs and how recounts 
are to be conducted in city districts. 
2. From the Department of Revenue Administration:  guidance on how the "central office 
administrative budget" is defined and how an adopted cap interacts with existing charter and 
municipal caps. 
 
3. From the General Court: amendments in the 2027 session, before the question returns to the 
ballot in November 2028, that resolve these ambiguities. We also ask that the ballot language be 
reviewed so that voters understand the property tax cap applies to the district's entire levy, not 
only to central office administration. 
 
We recognize that state leaders are balancing real pressure on property taxpayers, and we share the 
goal of spending public money carefully. Manchester already lives under a tax cap, and we know what it 
takes to plan a budget within one. That experience is why we ask for clarity. Our district serves nearly

12,000 students, over 53% of whom qualify for Free and Reduced Meals, 20% of whom are Multilingual 
Learners, and 23% of whom receive special education services. Districts like ours, and the smaller 
districts around us, need to know the rules before they write the budgets those students depend on. 
 
Thank you for your attention to these questions. We would welcome the chance to share Manchester's 
experience with a long-standing tax cap and to work with you on clear guidance. 
 
Respectfully,

Guidance on HB 1300 
 
What is HB1300 and What Does it Do? 
Under newly enacted HB 1300, now codified as RSA 32:5-i, voters at the November 2026 
and November 2028 state general elections will be presented with a single ballot question 
concerning two separate limitations:(1) a local property tax cap for the school district; 
and (2) a fixed cap on the SAU central office administrative budget. The form of the 
ballot question is prescribed by law and will appear on the state general election ballot.  
Although both limitations are included in a single ballot question, whether each limitation 
is adopted is determined separately. 
If three-fifths (3/5) of the voters voting on the question in the municipalities and wards 
served by a school district vote in favor, the school district local tax cap is adopted. The 
cap limits the amount of local property taxes that may be raised for the school district.  
Separately, if three-fifths (3/5) of the voters voting on the question in the municipalities and 
wards served by the school administrative unit vote in favor, the SAU fixed cap is 
adopted. The SAU cap limits the “central office administrative budget” 1 to 6% of the total 
school district appropriations of the districts comprising the SAU, excluding bonded 
capital costs as provided in the statute.  
 
1 The services and expenditures which comprise the “school administrative unit central office administrative 
budget” as defined in RSA 32:5-i, IX do not include all of the “superintendent services” listed in RSA 194-C:4, 
or Ed 302, nor does it include all of the services and expenditures required under 194-C:9 (as amended by 
HB564) to be included in a SAU budget. In the event the HB1300 ballot question passes in your SAU, and 
absent guidance from the DRA or NHED, districts and SAUs should consult with private counsel as to how to 
apply the 32:5-i limitation your SAU budget. 
5
NHSBA©2026  Page 2 
Because the school district and SAU votes are calculated separately, particularly in a 
multi-district SAU, it is possible for the school district tax cap to be adopted while the SAU 
cap is not, or vice versa.  
How Is the School District Tax Cap Calculated? 
The school district tax cap limits the amount of local property taxes that may be raised for 
the school district. The statute establishes the following formula for determining the 
maximum allowable levy: 
Prior fiscal year property tax levy × (1 + inflation + net new taxable property growth)  
The statute defines both "inflation" and "net new taxable property growth," provides for the 
exclusion of certain bonded capital costs, and directs the Department of Revenue 
Administration (DRA) to annually certify net new taxable property growth.  
A cap approved at the November 2026 election first applies beginning with the FY 2028 
school district or SAU budget, as applicable. A cap approved at the November 2028 
election first applies beginning with the FY 2030 budget.  
How Will HB 1300 Impact Different School Districts? 
There is no single answer to this question. How HB 1300 will operate in a particular school 
district depends upon a variety of factors and, in some circumstances, provisions of the 
law are unclear. 
Among the factors that may affect how the law applies are whether a school district is: 
 a single-district SAU or part of a multi-district SAU; 
 a cooperative school district or a single-municipality school district; 
 a district operating under a charter; 
 an SB2 district, and if so whether it is operating under a default budget; 
 a district already subject to a tax or budget cap; and/or 
 a city school district and, if so, the governmental and fiscal structure under which 
the district operates (for instance, is it “city dependent” or “independent”). 
The statute expressly provides that it does not repeal, supersede, or diminish an existing 
property tax limitation that is more restrictive. It further provides that where more than one 
applicable property tax or budget limitation applies, each applicable limitation must be 
satisfied.  
6
NHSBA©2026  Page 3 
HB 1300 also contains different provisions for districts with an annual meeting and 
districts without an annual meeting. Application of those provisions, particularly to certain 
city school districts and districts governed by charters, raises questions that may depend 
upon the circumstances of the individual district.  
For these and other issues on which the language of the statute is unclear, NHSBA 
recommends that school boards consult with their own legal counsel rather than rely upon 
generalized guidance concerning how the statute should be interpreted and applied within 
a specific district or SAU. 
Electioneering and HB 1300  
Because HB 1300 will appear as a question on the November general election ballot, 
school boards and employees should be mindful of New Hampshire's electioneering laws. 
RSA 659:44-a prohibits a public employee from electioneering while performing official 
duties and from using government property or equipment for electioneering. 
“Electioneering” includes communications that a reasonable person would believe 
explicitly advocate for or against a measure being voted upon. RSA 659:44-a. 
School district employees 
 DO provide factual, neutral information concerning HB 1300 and relevant district 
financial information as part of official duties.  
 DON'T advocate for a “Yes” or “No” vote while performing official duties or use 
district equipment, email accounts, or other government property for 
electioneering. RSA 659:44-a expressly prohibits both.  
School board members 
Elected and appointed school board members are expressly excluded from the definition 
of “public employee” incorporated into RSA 659:44-a.  
 DO participate in public discussion of HB 1300 and provide relevant factual 
information concerning its potential impact on the district.  
 DON'T assume that the exclusion from RSA 659:44-a resolves all questions 
concerning advocacy by a board or individual board members acting in their 
official capacity, particularly when district resources are involved. Boards should 
consult legal counsel regarding such questions.  
 Board members MAY, however, advocate for a “Yes” or “No” when acting and 
speaking in their personal capacities and without using district resources.  
7
NHSBA©2026  Page 4 
District resources2 
 DO use district resources to provide factual and educational information about HB 
1300 and its potential impact.  
 DON'T use district resources to produce or distribute materials expressly 
advocating for or against the ballot question, or direct district employees to use 
district resources for prohibited electioneering. 
Questions concerning the permissible scope of advocacy by a school board or individual 
board members, particularly when district funds or resources are involved, should be 
referred to local legal counsel. 
Public Hearings and Informational Forums 
HB 1300 expressly permits school boards and SAU boards to one or more public hearing 
on the local tax cap and the SAU fixed cap on central office administrative budgets.  
Because this school district related issue is removed from the ordinary annual meeting 
process, such hearings may be the only opportunity for the Board and the public to explore 
and discuss the new law and what it could mean to your districts. If your school board is 
considering holding a public hearing or informational forum, NHSBA offers the following 
suggestions: 
 Provide sufficient advance notice to the public. Unlike many statutory hearings, 
there are no specific notice requirements beyond those of RSA 91-A. Given that the 
ballot vote is on November 3 (absentee ballots go out earlier), you would want to 
schedule your hearing at least a week prior.  
 Establish clear rules for the meeting. Consider whether the board's regular public 
comment policy is appropriate for the hearing or forum, or whether additional or 
revised rules of order should be established.  NHSBA has attached a sample rules 
template at pages 7-8 of this guidance document. 
 Consider asking the school district moderator to moderate the hearing or 
forum. 
 Provide relevant financial information. This might include the current budget, 
projected budget, fixed costs, estimated revenues, the current local property tax 
 
2 The restriction against board members using district resources does not apply to such things as advocating 
by using microphones at board meetings or public hearings, nor for preparation and delivery of informational 
flyers or videos, although it  would apply to printing advocacy flyers or using district resources to prepare 
advocacy videos.  
8
NHSBA©2026  Page 5 
levy, and other information that may assist voters in understanding the possible 
impact of the caps. 
 Consider providing illustrative scenarios or hypotheticals. These may help 
explain how adoption of either or both caps could affect future school district and 
SAU budgets. Any assumptions used in such examples should be clearly identified. 
 Keep the purpose of the hearing or forum educational. The objective should be to 
provide voters with factual information about HB 1300 and its potential impact on 
the school district and SAU if either or both limitations are adopted. 
 Be mindful of electioneering restrictions. The fact that RSA 32:5-i expressly 
permits a public hearing does not eliminate otherwise applicable election laws as 
described above. While board members and superintendents are not considered 
employees under the electioneering statutes, other employees participating as part 
of their official duties (e.g., business office employees, principals, etc.) remain 
subject to RSA 659:44-a's prohibition against electioneering while performing those 
duties. 
New Responsibilities for the SAU “Secretary” 
One of the more confounding aspects of HB 1300 is the role it assigns to the "secretary of 
the school administrative unit board." 
Among other things, RSA 32:5-i provides that: 
 the moderator of each municipality or ward in the school district shall report the 
results of the ballot question to the secretary of the SAU board for the school 
district; 
 the moderator of each municipality or ward in the SAU shall report the results to the 
secretary of the SAU board; and 
 the secretary of the SAU board shall certify the results to DRA.  
The statute also assigns the secretary responsibilities in connection with recounts. For a 
school district local tax cap recount, the statute provides that 10 registered voters from 
any municipality served by the school district may apply in writing to the school district 
clerk within seven days of the general election. It then provides that "the secretary" shall 
schedule the recount, which is to be conducted by the school board. For an SAU fixed-cap 
recount, the request is made to the secretary of the SAU, and the secretary schedules a 
recount to be conducted by the “SAU.”  
9
NHSBA©2026  Page 6 
Single-District SAUs Present an Additional Issue 
RSA 194-C:5 provides that the school board of each SAU shall meet annually and 
organize by choosing a chairperson, secretary, and treasurer.  
However, RSA 194-C:3 expressly provides that single-district SAUs are 
considered the same as a single school district and are exempt from the 
requirements of RSA chapter 194-C, except for the requirement to provide 
superintendent services under RSA 194-C:4. Thus, unlike a multi-district SAU, a 
single-district SAU is not required by RSA chapter 194-C to appoint an SAU 
secretary. RSA 194-C:3 Single District School Administrative Units; Exemption  
This creates an apparent issue under HB 1300, which assigns responsibilities to the 
"secretary of the school administrative unit board" without separately addressing 
how those responsibilities are to be performed in a single-district SAU that does not 
have such an officer.  
If a multi-district SAU does not presently have an appointed secretary, NHSBA 
recommends that the SAU board ensure that a secretary is appointed. 
For single-district SAUs, NHSBA recommends consulting with legal counsel 
concerning how the duties assigned by RSA 32:5-i to the "secretary of the school 
administrative unit board" should be performed. 
Limitation on NHSBA's Guidance 
HB 1300 contains numerous ambiguities and raises significant questions concerning its 
interpretation and implementation. In addition, how the law applies to an individual school 
district may depend upon factors particular to that district, including its form of 
government, SAU structure, charter provisions, existing tax or budget limitations, and other 
local circumstances. As of October 1, 2026, neither the Secretary of State’s Office nor the 
Attorney General’s Office have provided guidance relative to some of the issues/questions 
concerning the functions of the SAU secretaries, or district clerks relative to what is 
otherwise a state election conducted by municipal election officers. If and when such 
guidance is released, NHSBA will forward it to NHSBA members. 
For these reasons, NHSBA's guidance concerning HB 1300 is intentionally limited to 
the statute's plain and unambiguous provisions. Where the statute is unclear, NHSBA 
believes it is more appropriate to identify the issue than to attempt to resolve it for its 
members. 
NHSBA is aware that school districts and SAUs are consulting with their own legal counsel 
regarding implementation of the new law. School boards and SAU boards should likewise 
10
NHSBA©2026  Page 7 
consult with their legal counsel regarding questions about how RSA 32:5-i applies to their 
particular circumstances. 
Consistent with NHSBA's longstanding practice, NHSBA does not intend for this guidance 
to contradict or supplant advice provided by local counsel. This document is intended to 
provide general information to assist school boards as they navigate the requirements and 
uncertainties presented by HB 1300.

AN ACT establishing a school district local tax cap question for the state general elections of
2026 and 2028 and related limitations on central office administrative expenses in
school districts.
SPONSORS: Rep. Ankarberg, Straf. 7; Sen. Innis, Dist 7

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
AMENDED ANALYSIS
This bill:
I. Establishes a school district local tax cap question for the state general elections of 2026 and 2028.
II. Establishes limitations on central office administrative expenses in school districts.
III. Requires that the commissioner of the department of revenue administration adopt rules relative
to the school district local tax cap question and limitations on central office administrative expenses in
school districts.

STATE OF NEW HAMPSHIRE
In the Year of Our Lord Two Thousand Twenty-Six
AN ACT establishing a school district local tax cap question for the state general elections of
2026 and 2028 and related limitations on central office administrative expenses in
school districts.
Be it Enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives in General Court convened:
324:1 New Section; Municipal Budget Law; Preparation of Budgets; School District Local Tax Cap
and School Administrative Fixed Cap on Central Office Administrative Budgets. Amend RSA 32 by
inserting after section 5-h the following new section:
32:5-i School District Local Tax Cap and School Administrative Fixed Cap on Central Office
Administrative Budgets.
I. During the November 2026 and November 2028 state general elections, every town and ward
in a city shall conduct a vote on a local tax cap question for their school district and a fixed cap on the
school administrative unit central office administrative budget. The question shall appear on the ballot by
operation of law and shall not require a warrant article, citizen petition, or separate local legislative
approval.
II. The question required under paragraph I shall be printed on the state general election ballot
administered pursuant to RSA 656:13, following the offices columns. If the secretary of state determines
that sufficient space on the front of the state general election ballot does not permit inclusion of the
question, the secretary of state shall cause the question to be printed on the reverse side of the state
general election ballot and shall cause a notice to be printed on the front of the ballot directing voters to
turn the ballot over to vote on the question. If the secretary of state determines that printing on the
reverse side is also impracticable, the question shall be printed on a separate official ballot to be
distributed, cast, collected, and counted at the same polling place and during the same hours as the state
general election ballot. The secretary of state shall adopt any procedures necessary to ensure that ballot
counting devices used pursuant to RSA 656:40 are programmed to read and count votes cast on both
sides of the ballot where the reverse side is used.
III. Nothing in this section shall prohibit a municipality, school board, or school administrative unit
board from holding a public hearing on the question for the local tax cap and for the school administrative
fixed cap on central office administrative budgets.
IV. Whenever the question required under paragraph I is printed on the state general election
ballot or on a separate official ballot pursuant to paragraph II, the secretary of state shall ensure that said
question is also included on all applicable absentee ballots consistent with RSA 656:36.

V. The school district local tax cap and school administrative unit fixed cap question on the ballot
for towns and wards with an annual school district meeting shall read:
“Shall the [name of municipality] limit property tax growth for [name(s) of school district(s)] under RSA
32:5-i? If adopted for a two-year period: (1) the local property tax levy may not grow beyond the prior
year’s amount, adjusted for inflation and new construction; (2) SAU central office spending may not
exceed 6 percent of total school district appropriations; and (3) bonded capital costs are excluded from
both limits. These caps apply only to administrative operations of the SAU central office and do not affect
classroom instruction, school-based services, or other municipal expenditures. These limits may be
overridden as provided in RSA 32:5-i. Adoption requires a three-fifths (3/5) majority vote.”
Towns and wards serving more than one school district shall include the names of all such school districts
in the question.
VI.(a) The moderator of each municipality or ward in the school district shall report the results
on the question to the secretary of the school administrative unit board for the school district. If a 3/5
majority of the voters voting in the municipalities and wards served by the school district approve the
question, then the maximum allowable levy per the local tax cap for the district under paragraph VIII shall
be binding.
(b) The moderator of each municipality or ward in the school administrative unit shall report
the results on the question to the secretary of the school administrative unit board served by the
municipality or ward. If a 3/5 majority of the voters voting in the municipalities and wards served by the
school administrative unit approve the question, then the SAU fixed cap for the SAU central office
administrative budget under paragraph IX shall be binding.
(c) The secretary of the school administrative unit board shall certify the results of the votes
to the department of revenue administration. Preservation of ballots shall be pursuant to RSA 33-A:3-a,
XXXVII.
VII.(a) Any 10 registered voters from any municipality served by a school district, before the
expiration of 7 days from the date of the general election, may apply in writing to the school district clerk
for a recount of the ballots for the question on a school district local tax cap under this section. The
secretary shall schedule a recount, to be conducted by the school board, not earlier than 5 days nor later
than 10 days after the date the secretary receives the petition. The applicants for such a recount shall pay
to the school clerk a fee of $10 for conducting the recount.
(b) Any 10 registered voters from any municipality served by a school administrative unit,
before the expiration of 7 days from the date of the general election, may apply in writing to the secretary
of the school administrative unit for a recount of the ballots for the question on a school administrative unit
fixed cap under this section. The secretary shall schedule a recount, to be conducted by the school
administrative unit, not earlier than 5 days nor later than 10 days after the date the secretary receives the
petition. The applicants for such a recount shall pay to the secretary of the school administrative unit
board a fee of $10 for conducting the recount.

IX. In the municipalities and wards served by a school administrative unit where the school
administrative unit fixed cap question under this section is approved by the voters, the fixed cap for school
administrative unit central office administrative budgets shall be 6 percent of the sum of the total school
district appropriation amounts, except costs of bonded capital projects pursuant to paragraph XVI, in the
school districts comprising the SAU. “School administrative unit central office administrative budgets”
means expenditures for the general management and administration of a school administrative unit.
These expenditures include superintendent services; assistant or deputy superintendent services;
business administration; human resources; finance; payroll; purchasing; district-level information
technology administration; legal services; public relations; and other non-school-based administrative
functions, regardless of physical location or building assignment. The term also includes district-level
curriculum directors, directors of instruction, or similarly titled positions who are not employed under a
collective bargaining agreement or who do not provide direct classroom instruction for more than 50
percent of their work time, as well as any personnel reported to the department of education as employed
by the central office. The term does not include school-based administrative staff; classroom instruction;
instructional support services; special education services; transportation; food services; or facilities
operations and maintenance.

X. The legislative body may vote to exceed the school district local tax cap or the school
administrative unit fixed cap using the override procedures provided in these subparagraphs.
(a) The provisions of this subparagraph shall apply only to districts with an annual meeting.
The legislative body may override the school district local tax cap under paragraph VIII, or the school
administrative unit fixed cap under paragraph IX, by the usual procedures applicable to annual meetings
of the legislative body, provided that: when a proposed appropriation will cause the cap to be exceeded or
the cap has already been exceeded, exclusive of bonded costs defined in paragraph XVI, voting on the
appropriation question shall be by ballot, but the question shall not be placed on the official ballot used to
elect officers, except in the case of a legislative body that uses an official ballot form of meeting under
RSA 40:13 or under a charter adopted pursuant to RSA 49-D. If a 3/5 majority or the super majority as
determined under a charter pursuant to RSA 49-D of those voting on the question vote "yes," the
appropriation is approved. Only votes in the affirmative or negative shall be included in the calculation of
the 3/5 majority or the super majority as determined under a charter pursuant to RSA 49-D.
(b) The provisions of this subparagraph shall apply only to districts without an annual
meeting. If the school district local tax cap has been adopted, the legislative body shall adopt a school
district budget, exclusive of bonded costs defined in paragraph XVI, that does not exceed the local tax cap
established under paragraph VIII, unless the legislative body overrides the cap by the supermajority
defined in its charter pursuant to RSA 49-C:33, I(d) or RSA 49-D:3, I(e). If the school administrative unit
fixed cap has been adopted, the legislative body overrides that cap by the supermajority defined in its
charter pursuant to RSA 49-C:33, I(d) or RSA 49-D:3, I(e).
XI. No municipal tax rate shall be set that causes a taxing authority to exceed its certified limits
under this section.
(a) For a school district that has adopted the school district local tax cap or a school
administrative unit that has adopted the school administrative unit fixed cap under this section, the
governing body shall forward, at a time and in a form prescribed by the department of revenue
administration, documentation demonstrating compliance with the adopted caps. Such documentation
shall include:
(1) The computation of the school district local tax cap or school administrative unit fixed
cap for the applicable year;
(2) Proposed appropriations by the governing body and budget committee and estimated
revenues going into the annual meeting, showing the estimated amount of property taxes to be raised for
the school district budget or school administrative unit central office administrative budgets, or both;
(3) Appropriations voted by the annual or special meeting of the legislative body; and
(4) The count of any ballot votes taken to override the school district local tax cap or
school administrative unit fixed cap.
(b) Upon review of documentation submitted under subparagraph (a), if the commissioner of
the department of revenue administration determines that the certified school district budget results in
estimated taxes exceeding the adopted school administrative unit fixed cap and that no valid override vote

XII. If approved at the November 2026 state general election, the school district local tax cap or
the school administrative unit fixed cap, or both, shall apply beginning with the fiscal year 2028 school
district total budget or school administrative unit budget, as applicable. If approved at the November 2028
state general election, the school district local tax cap or the school administrative unit fixed cap, or both,
shall apply beginning with the fiscal year 2030 school district total budget or school administrative unit
budget, as applicable.
XIII. Any taxpayer in a member school district or school district of the school administrative unit,
as applicable, shall have standing to enforce this section in superior court.
XIV. Nothing in this section may be construed to repeal, supersede, or diminish any property tax
limitation that is more restrictive under existing law, a municipal charter, or a local ordinance. When more
than one property tax limitation, tax cap, local tax cap, or budget cap applies, each applicable limitation
must be fully satisfied.
XV. This section shall operate solely as a local tax cap limitation on the estimated amount of local
taxes to be raised for the fiscal year attributable to the school district or a fixed cap on the school
administrative unit central office administrative budget, as applicable.
XVI.(a) Bonded capital costs shall include principal or interest on bonds or notes only if the
bonded indebtedness is issued solely for the acquisition, construction, or major structural renovation of
real property, reported pursuant to RSA 198:4-a.
(b) The department of revenue administration shall certify annually the portion of debt service
that qualifies for exclusion.
(c) No exclusion shall apply unless certified by the department.
